passages.happening:
While Peter and John are still speaking to the people, “the priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them, greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead” (verses 1-2).

They seize Peter and John and, because it is evening, put them in custody until the next day. “But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The captain of the temple guard was a senior priest who kept order in the temple. Under him served Levites, men of the tribe set apart for temple work, who acted as the temple's police. This was not the Roman army. It was the temple's own guard.

The Sadducees were a small, powerful group drawn from the leading priestly and wealthy families around the temple. They held only to the written law and said there is no resurrection (23:8). So the apostles' message offended them twice over: these untrained men were teaching in the temple, and they were teaching that the resurrection had already begun, in Jesus.

It was evening, so the two were held until morning.

Luke sets the arrest and the growth side by side. The leaders lock up two men; the number of believing men grows to about five thousand. It will be the pattern of the whole book. The word is not bound.
passages.ot: The hope of resurrection the Sadducees denied was already in the Scriptures: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). The Pharisees believed it. What was new in the apostles' preaching was the claim that it had already begun with one man.
passages.asks: The leaders were most disturbed not by a healing but by a message: that death has been broken. Ask whether the resurrection is, for you, a doctrine you agree with or news that changes how you live. And notice that opposition did not stop the growth. It never does in Acts.

passages.t: Before the council: no other name
passages.happening:
The next day the rulers, elders and teachers of the law gather in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and others of the high priest's family. They ask, “By what power or what name did you do this?” (verse 7).

Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answers. If they are being examined “about a kind service to a man who was lame”, then let everyone know: “It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed” (verse 10).

“This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
This was the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders (leading men of the people) and scribes (experts in the law), led by the high priest. Many of these men had handed Jesus over to Pilate a few months before.

Caiaphas was the high priest that year. Annas, his father-in-law, had been high priest years before and was still called by the title and still had great influence (Luke 3:2; John 18:13). Nothing is known of John and Alexander. One old manuscript reads ‘Jonathan’ instead of ‘John’, and a son of Annas called Jonathan later became high priest, but most think ‘John’ is the original reading.

Peter's answer is bold, and a little ironic. They are on trial for doing a kindness. He uses their own question, ‘what name?’, to name Jesus.

A cornerstone was the main stone of a building, set at the corner to hold the walls true. The builders here are the council, the leaders of God's house. The stone they threw away, God has made the most important stone of all.
passages.ot: Peter quotes Psalm 118: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). Jesus had quoted the same verse about himself to the same leaders in the temple (Luke 20:17). Isaiah, too, spoke of a stone God would lay in Zion: “a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16).
passages.hard:
‘There is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved’ (verse 12). The verse says plainly that salvation comes through Jesus alone. That is the text's claim, and it should be read as it stands. Jesus said the same: “No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). Christians confess it.

Many people today hear this as arrogant. It helps to see the setting. Peter is not a powerful man forcing his faith on the weak; he is a prisoner on trial before the powerful. He is not saying Christians are better than other people, but that God has acted in one person, for everyone. The name is given ‘to men’, to all people, under heaven.

A different question is what happens to people who never hear the name. Christians differ on that question, and the Bible does not answer it in so many words. Some hold that only those who hear and believe will be saved. Others hold that God may save some who never heard, still only through Christ, in ways known to God. These notes do not settle it. The site's Honest Answer ‘What about those who never heard of Jesus?’ sets out the main views and what each has to face.
passages.asks: Peter turned an inquiry about a kindness into a chance to name Jesus. Ask whether there are questions people ask you, about why you do what you do, that are really an opening. And if you believe what verse 12 says, ask who around you has not yet heard the name.

passages.happening:
The council sees the boldness of Peter and John and realizes “that they were unschooled, ordinary men” (verse 13). They are amazed, and they recognize that these men had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing there, they have nothing to say.

They send the apostles out and talk among themselves. “It is clear to everyone living in Jerusalem that a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it” (verse 16). But to stop the message spreading, they order them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

“But Peter and John replied, ‘Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard’” (verses 19-20). After more threats, the council lets them go, because all the people are praising God for what has happened. The healed man is over forty years old.
passages.hearers:
‘Unschooled, ordinary men’ does not have to mean the apostles could not read. The first word most likely means men without formal training in the law under a recognized teacher; some think it may mean they could not read or write, which was common then and no shame. The second word means laymen, private people with no official standing. The leaders had said the same of Jesus: “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” (John 7:15).

Notice what the council admits in private: ‘we cannot deny it’. They do not dispute the miracle. They simply do not want it talked about.

Peter and John do not shout, run or fight. They answer calmly, ask the council to judge for itself, and say they are witnesses who cannot keep silent about what they saw. That is all a witness can do.
passages.ot: Israel's Scriptures hold stories of faithful people who refused a ruler's command when it meant disobeying God. The Hebrew midwives in Egypt “feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live” (Exodus 1:17). Daniel's three friends told the king of Babylon, “we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up” (Daniel 3:18). Daniel kept praying three times a day when the law forbade it (Daniel 6:10).
passages.hard:
Does ‘listen to you rather than God’ (verse 19), and later ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (5:29), give Christians permission to disobey any law they dislike? No. The apostles refused one command: to stop speaking about Jesus. They did not refuse the council's authority in other things. They answered respectfully, did not resist arrest, and later took a beating without striking back (5:40-41). They prayed for courage, not for revenge.

The New Testament also tells believers to respect those in authority: “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities” (Romans 13:1), and “fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). Christians differ on how these fit together when a government commands what is wrong. Many hold that believers obey rulers in everything except when told to sin or forbidden to do what God commands, and then they refuse openly and peacefully and accept the cost. Others hold that Christians may also resist unjust laws in public, peaceful ways, for the sake of others who are wronged, and point to Christians who did so in movements against injustice. Some traditions also have long teaching on when, if ever, lawful resistance to a tyrant is right. These notes do not settle these questions, and they apply this verse to no modern political cause. The site's guide ‘Does Romans 13 Mean Christians Must Obey Every Government?’ looks at them further.
passages.asks: The apostles' boldness came from one thing: they had been with Jesus, and they had seen what they had seen. Ask whether people around you can tell that you have been with Jesus. And ask what you would do if you were told to stop speaking of him: whether you would argue, hide, or simply, respectfully, keep going.

passages.happening:
Peter and John go back to their own people and tell them everything. Together the believers lift their voices to God. They call him ‘Sovereign Lord’ and say, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them” (verse 24).

They pray the words of Psalm 2, “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” and say that in this very city “Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus” (verse 27). They did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand.

“And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness” (verse 29), as God stretches out his hand to heal. When they have prayed, the place where they are meeting is shaken, “and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
‘Sovereign Lord’ translates a Greek word for a master with full authority. The believers begin not with their danger but with who God is: the maker of everything. Next to him, the council's threats look small.

The Herod named here is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, before whom Jesus was sent during his trial (Luke 23:7-12). Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor. The prayer names everyone: the Jewish ruler, the Roman governor, the Gentiles and the people of Israel. All stood together against Jesus. No one group carries the blame alone.

Notice what they do not ask for. They do not ask for the threats to stop, or for their enemies to be punished. They ask for boldness to keep speaking, and for God to keep healing.
passages.ot:
The prayer opens with words close to the Ten Commandments and the Psalms: the Lord “made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (Exodus 20:11; compare Psalm 146:6).

Then it quotes Psalm 2:1-2: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One”. ‘Anointed One’ is Messiah, Christ. The believers read the psalm as fulfilled in Jesus' trial, when rulers gathered against God's anointed King.
passages.asks: Under threat, they prayed for courage, not comfort. Ask what you pray for when you are afraid. Ask too whether your prayers begin with your problem or with God. Theirs began with the God who made the sea, and the room shook.

passages.happening:
“The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned” (verse 32). With great power the apostles go on telling of the resurrection, and grace is on them all.

“There were no needy ones among them” (verse 34). Those who own land or houses sell them, bring the money, and lay it at the apostles' feet, and it is given to anyone in need.

One of them is Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles call Barnabas, which means Son of Encouragement. He sells a field he owns and lays the money at the apostles' feet (verses 36-37).
passages.hearers:
To lay something ‘at someone's feet’ was a sign of handing it over to that person's care. The money was put in the apostles' hands to give out.

This was now a church of thousands (verse 4). The richer believers sold property as needs came up, so that no one went without.

Barnabas is introduced with care, because he will matter later. He is the man who stands up for Saul when everyone else is afraid of him (9:27), and who travels with Paul. He was a Levite, from the tribe set apart for the temple. The Law said Levites would have no share of the land as the other tribes did (Numbers 18:20), yet Scripture shows men of priestly families owning fields; the prophet Jeremiah, from a family of priests, bought one (Jeremiah 32:9). Barnabas gives his away.
passages.ot: “There were no needy ones among them” echoes the Law's hope: “There will be no poor among you, however, because the LORD will surely bless you in the land” (Deuteronomy 15:4). The same chapter of Deuteronomy, being honest about a fallen world, says that the poor will always be in the land, and so commands, “open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). The first church did just that.
passages.hard:
Was this a law that all believers had to give up their property? No. The next chapter makes it plain that each person's land was his own, and the money was his to use; Peter says so to Ananias (5:4). People sold property when there was need, not all at once. Barnabas is named because his gift was worth noticing. The sharing was free and generous, not forced.

These verses have been claimed over the years for many modern economic and political programs, from more than one side. These notes make no such application of any kind, left or right. Luke is describing a church, not a government, and believers giving freely out of love, not a system. What the passage asks of every church is that believers care for one another so well that no one among them goes without.
passages.asks: The first believers held their possessions loosely because they held each other tightly. Ask whether anything you own has a stronger grip on you than the needs of the people you worship with. And ask who, in your church, might be quietly going without.
